findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so blocks are trivially bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs an exact-match query: BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first. The email passed in comes straight from the signup form via User.new_from_params (which does no downcasing), and the blocked_emails table stores whatever case the admin entered. A spammer blocked as 'bad@spam.com' can register successfully as 'BAD@spam.com' or 'Bad@Spam.com' because the lookup won't match, and the user's own email uniqueness check is also case-sensitive so it won't collide with an existing account either. The block list should normalize (strip + downcase) both the stored value and the queried value, or the query should be case-insensitive.

findings.title: match_count increment in should_block? is a racy read-modify-write
findings.body: When a blocked email matches, should_block? does record.match_count += 1; record.save. Under concurrent signups hitting the same blocked address (the exact scenario a block list exists for), two processes can read the same match_count and both write back the same incremented value, losing counts. Use an atomic update (e.g., update_counters or UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1) instead. Additionally, calling full record.save here re-runs validations on every match and silently drops the stat update if the save fails for any reason; the return value is still computed from the stale record, which is fine, but the statistics become unreliable without any signal.

findings.title: should_block? writes to the database from inside a model validation
findings.body: EmailValidator#validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value), which increments match_count and saves the blocked_emails row as a side effect of running validations. This means any user.valid? call — including ones that never lead to a save, and repeated client-side-driven validation attempts — mutates persistent statistics, and the write happens outside the user's save transaction. If stats collection is intended, it would be safer to record the match only when a signup is actually rejected (e.g., in the controller or in an after-validation hook gated on the record being persisted), otherwise the counters can be inflated arbitrarily by repeatedly triggering validation without ever creating an account.

findings.title: Moved whitelist/blacklist email validation has no specs in the new validator spec
findings.body: The email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic was moved out of User#email_validator into the new EmailValidator class, but the newly added spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb only covers the BlockedEmail branch — there are no tests exercising the whitelist or blacklist paths of the moved code. If no existing user specs cover those site settings, a regression there (e.g., in email_in_restriction_setting?) would go unnoticed; the spec file should include cases for whitelist-allowed, whitelist-rejected, and blacklist-rejected emails.
